stem: What does Joseph's message show about the Nez Perce flight of 1877?

stimulus.source_note: Chief Joseph's surrender message, Bear Paw Mountains, Montana Territory, October 1877, as transcribed by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood, aide to General Howard; printed in Harper's Weekly, November 17, 1877. Public domain. Text verified against the University of Washington Libraries transcription of Harper's Weekly and the National Park Service account of the Nez Perce surrender.
stimulus.text:
Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, surrender message, Bear Paw Mountains, Montana Territory, October 1877 (as transcribed by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood; ellipses mark omissions):

"Tell General Howard I know his heart. What he told me before I have in my heart. I am tired of fighting. Our chiefs are killed. Looking Glass is dead. Tu-hul-hul-sote is dead. The old men are all dead. It is the young men who say yes or no. He who led the young men is dead. It is cold and we have no blankets. The little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food. No one knows where they are - perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children, and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever."

options.text: It was a planned invasion of Montana Territory
options.misconception: Background: the Nez Perce were fleeing toward Canada after being ordered onto a reservation; they were not invading Montana.

options.text: It was a desperate retreat by families, not an army
It was a religious pilgrimage led by a prophet
options.misconception: Background: the Ghost Dance was the religious movement of the period; the Nez Perce flight was a flight from soldiers.

options.text: It was a trading journey that accidentally met the army
options.misconception: Background: the Nez Perce had been fighting and fleeing the army for months before the surrender.

rationales.A: Background: the Nez Perce were fleeing toward Canada after being ordered onto a reservation. They were not invading Montana.
rationales.B: Joseph speaks of children freezing, people run away to the hills, and a search for his own children among the dead. This is a community fleeing, with families and elders, not a war party.
rationales.C: Background: the Ghost Dance was the religious movement of the period. The Nez Perce flight was a flight from soldiers.
rationales.D: Background: the Nez Perce had been fighting and fleeing the army for months before the surrender.
rationales.general:
Picture a column of people, not soldiers, moving through the mountains toward Canada.
1. Notice who Joseph talks about. Children, old men, families run away to the hills.
2. Notice what he wants. Time to look for his children, and to see how many he can find among the dead.
3. Name the flight for what it was. A whole community retreating, carrying its families with it.
Remember: in a people's war, the fighters and the families travel together, and both pay the price.
